text: Antonio Giolitti (12 February 1915 – 8 February 2010) was an Italian politician and cabinet member. He was the grandson of Giovanni Giolitti, the well-known liberal statesman of the pre-fascist period who served as Prime Minister of Italy five times. Giolitti was born in Rome. He joined the Italian Communist Party (Partito Comunista Italiano, or PCI) in 1940 and was arrested and tried by the fascist regime but acquitted for his associations with them. In the spring of 1943, he resumed his clandestine activities for the Communist Party, contacting numerous military and political personalities to plan the overthrow of the fascist regime. During the Italian Resistance in World War II, Giolitti was seriously wounded in combat and was sent to France to recover, remaining unable to return to Italy until after the end of the conflict. After the war, he was involved in significant political activity: he served as junior minister to the foreign minister in Ferruccio Parri's government, was a communist deputy to the Constituent Assembly, and was elected to the Chamber of Deputies in the PCI lists in 1948 and 1953. In 1957, he left the Communist Party following the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising and the Manifesto of the 101, then joined the Italian Socialist Party. Giolitti held ministerial positions in several Italian governments: he was Minister for the Budget from 1963 to 1964, from 1969 to 1972, and from 1973 to 1974, in the administrations led by Aldo Moro, Mariano Rumor, and Emilio Colombo, respectively, where he inspired Italian economic planning. From 1977 to 1985, he was a member of the Executive Commission of the European Economic Community in Brussels, responsible for Regional Policy. In 1987, he left the Italian Socialist Party due to disagreements with its leader Bettino Craxi and returned to the Italian Communist Party as an independent candidate, being elected to the Italian Senate. At the end of his parliamentary term, he withdrew from active politics. Giolitti authored political texts and published a book with his memoirs in 1992. He also participated actively in Italian cultural life, having served as an advisor to publisher Giulio Einaudi in his youth and collaborating with cultural magazines such as Lettera Internazionale. In 2006, he was awarded the Cavaliere di Gran Croce, the highest honour conferred by the President of the Italian Republic, and died in Rome on 8 February 2010.
